abstract: The logic of RNA-based silencing involves nascent RNA molecules that serve as scaffolds to recruit proteins that repress transcription. Despite transcription and silencing being antagonistic, RNA-based recruitment mechanisms have been widely adopted in organisms ranging from yeast to humans. In fission yeast (Schizosaccharomyces pombe), the nuclear RNAi pathway that establishes heterochromatin at pericentromeric repeats to silence transcription exemplifies this paradox. Current models propose that cells reconcile these opposing activities by confining pericentromeric transcription to S phase while maintaining silencing during the rest of the cell cycle. Here, using strand-specific single-molecule RNA FISH (smFISH), we detect forward and reverse pericentromeric transcripts with high sensitivity and single-cell resolution. We find that repeat-associated transcription is rare, heterogeneous and happens independently of cell-cycle control. Instead, transcript production is governed solely by feedback involving small RNA biogenesis and H3K9 methylation. By combining mathematical modeling with experiments, we show that low levels of H3K9me or siRNAs prevent heterochromatin establishment, whereas high levels of H3K9me cause stochastic switching. Our work reveals that the same RNA-based feedback architecture can sample distinct transcriptional regimes, with feedback strength determining how often cells produce transcripts without any external regulatory inputs.
